needs.need: A HIPAA business associate agreement (BAA) has to be available on the cheapest plan, because the big vendors only give one on enterprise tiers that solo and small practices cannot afford.
needs.who: Healthcare: solo therapists, small clinics and other small practices that send intake and consent paperwork
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, page not opened. Adobe Community threads on getting a BAA for Acrobat Sign, as relayed by the search tool: obtaining one "carries a greater than 4-fold increase in price just to obtain a BAA"; a poster asks "how can a small business (such as myself being a solo mental health provider in private practice) afford that"; another lists other services with a BAA and says "None of these services require an exorbitant 'enterprise' fee to sign a BAA." Thread 'BAA for HIPAA compliance, why is this so hard': https://community.adobe.com/t5/adobe-acrobat-sign-discussions/baa-for-hipaa-compliance-why-is-this-so-hard/td-p/13764645 (the search tool did not say which of the Adobe BAA threads each line came from). Hushmail blog (a competitor): "DocuSign will give you a BAA, but only with their enterprise account." https://blog.hushmail.com/blog/docusign-hipaa-compliant
needs.what_good_looks_like: The BAA is included in the $9 plan (or a clearly priced small add-on), stated on the pricing page, with no sales call and no plan upgrade.

needs.need: The BAA must be signable inside the product at signup, because people pay for a HIPAA-capable plan and then cannot use it while they wait for the vendor to execute or switch on the BAA.
needs.who: Healthcare: small practices that have already decided to pay for compliance
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, page not opened. Adobe Community BAA threads, as relayed by the search tool: a user "signed up for the enterprise plan, paid for it and cannot use it because I need to sign the BAA to be HIPAA compliant." https://community.adobe.com/t5/adobe-acrobat-sign-discussions/baa-for-hipaa-compliance-why-is-this-so-hard/td-p/13764645 . A comparison page returned by the same search run (the tool did not say which; candidates are https://signatures.com/buyers-guides/which-e-signature-platforms-support-hipaa-compliance-and-at-what-tier/ and https://www.hipaakit.co/blog/is-docusign-hipaa-compliant ) describes signNow HIPAA as "disabled by default; requires contacting SignNow support to execute a BAA before use." Adobe help page says "not all accounts will qualify for enablement": https://helpx.adobe.com/lv/sign/using/adobesign-hipaa-settings.html
needs.what_good_looks_like: A click-through BAA that is countersigned instantly, downloadable as a PDF for the practice's compliance file, and HIPAA mode is active the same minute.

needs.need: Signers in long, multi-page packets miss fields or fill everything in and never press the final finish button, so the document is not saved and the deal is delayed.
needs.who: Real estate agents whose clients are not confident with technology; applies to any trade sending long packets
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, pages not opened. Capterra dotloop reviews, as relayed by the search tool: for "tech adverse clients they struggle to fill out fields or how to complete/save a form"; clients fill everything out but never click the finish button so it does not save; signers scroll through long documents by hand, "which leads to missed signatures and delayed offers." https://www.capterra.com/p/136372/dotloop/reviews/?page=4 and https://www.capterra.com/p/136372/dotloop/reviews/
needs.what_good_looks_like: A guided signing flow that jumps to the next required field, shows "3 of 14 left", saves each field as it is completed, and finishes automatically (or with one unmissable prompt) when the last field is done. The sender sees "started but not finished" and can nudge.

needs.need: Two people who share one email address (married couples, elderly sellers) must each be able to sign as separate signers.
needs.who: Real estate agents with couples and elderly clients; also relevant to parents and guardians
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, pages not opened. Capterra dotloop reviews, as relayed by the search tool: an agent works with "elderly sellers who have only one email address, and dotloop requires a separate email for each signor"; another says when a husband and wife share one email they cannot each sign. https://www.capterra.com/p/136372/dotloop/reviews/ (review pages 2 to 8 were returned; the tool did not say which page)
needs.what_good_looks_like: Several signers can be sent to the same email address, each with their own named link and their own audit-trail entry, optionally told apart by SMS code or an access code.

needs.need: Signers must never be pushed to create an account after signing.
needs.who: Real estate agents and their clients; any signer who is a member of the public
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, page not opened. G2 dotloop reviews, as relayed by the search tool: clients get confused by a pop-up that "holds them hostage asking them if they want to create an account after signing." https://www.g2.com/products/dotloop/reviews?page=7
needs.what_good_looks_like: After the last signature the signer sees a plain "Done, a copy is in your email" screen with a download button. No signup prompt, no upsell.

needs.need: Bulk sending (the same offer letter or packet to many people) is locked to the top self-serve tier, and every send uses up quota even if the person never signs.
needs.who: HR and hiring teams at small organisations sending offer letters and onboarding packets; also schools and nonprofits sending one form to many people
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, pages not opened. Vendor pricing articles (competitors of DocuSign), as relayed by the search tool: "Business Pro at $40/user/month" is the plan that "unlocks features like advanced fields, payment collection through Stripe or Braintree, Bulk Send, and PowerForms"; "PowerForms and Bulk Send both count toward your envelope allowance on capped plans"; annual plans "include 100 envelopes per user per year" and every sent envelope counts even when the recipient never signs. https://verdocs.com/blog/docusign-pricing and https://meetergo.com/en/magazine/docusign-pricing (the tool did not say which line came from which). A G2 reviewer calls the sending plans very expensive for small businesses or casual users: https://www.g2.com/products/docusign/reviews?page=2
needs.what_good_looks_like: Bulk send from a spreadsheet is on the base plan. A signature is only charged when a document is completed; unsigned, declined and voided sends cost nothing. The price of a 40-person send is shown before sending.

needs.need: Payment has to be collectable at the moment of signing (retainer, deposit, quote acceptance) without buying the top tier or a second tool.
needs.who: Solo and small law firms collecting retainers with engagement letters; sales teams and tradespeople taking deposits on quotes
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, pages not opened. Sign-n-Pay blog (a vendor), as relayed by the search tool: "DocuSign Business Pro at $40 per user per month adds up quickly, and it still requires a separate payment collection tool." https://sign-n-pay.com/blog/e-signature-for-attorneys . Vendor pricing articles say payment collection through Stripe or Braintree is a Business Pro feature: https://verdocs.com/blog/docusign-pricing . A further result is titled "DocuSign Is Too Expensive for Most Small Law Firms. Here Are 6 Actual Alternatives.": https://www.swiftchecklist.com/blog/docusign-alternatives-for-small-law-firms
needs.what_good_looks_like: A payment field on any document on the base plan: signer signs, pays by card in the same screen, and both parties get the signed PDF plus a receipt. Money goes straight to the sender's own Stripe account.

needs.need: Senders need to see at a glance who has signed and who has not, without checking each document by hand.
needs.who: Real estate agents and transaction coordinators tracking many parties; office managers in any small organisation
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, pages not opened. A Capterra DocuSign reviewer, as relayed by the search tool, says the lack of native integration with project management software forces staff to check manually when documents are signed: https://www.capterra.com/p/121506/Docusign/reviews/?page=2 (pages 5, 6, 12, 28, 72 and 97 were also returned; the tool did not say which). On the positive side a G2 reviewer of DocuSign for Real Estate values that it tracks all parties: https://www.g2.com/products/docusign-for-real-estate/reviews
needs.what_good_looks_like: One list of open documents showing each signer's state (sent, opened, signed, declined), with an email or push the moment anyone signs and a one-tap reminder to whoever is holding things up.

needs.need: The signing page must work on whatever phone or old browser the signer has, because outdated browsers cause most signer problems.
needs.who: Real estate agents' clients; any signer on an older phone or computer
needs.evidence: Search-result excerpt only, page not opened. Dotloop's own blog, as relayed by the search tool, tells agents to ask clients early whether they will sign on a computer or a phone, and says updating the browser "often eliminates at least 90% of issues that clients run into when eSigning." https://www.dotloop.com/blog/2022/10/real-estate-client-esigning/
needs.what_good_looks_like: The signing page is plain, light and tested on old Safari, old Android browsers and in-app browsers (Gmail, Facebook). If the browser really cannot work, the signer is told exactly what to do instead of seeing a broken page.

needs.need: Preparing and sending a document from a phone has to be practical, not just signing on one.

needs.need: Senders lose when all they can show is a signature block or certificate and nobody can explain who sent the document, how it reached the signer, how the signature got onto the page and what each field means.
needs.who: Small businesses, lenders and employers who must prove a signature after the signer denies it, and their lawyers
needs.evidence: Fabian v. Renovate America (Cal. Ct. App. 2019, 42 Cal.App.5th 1062): the lender relied on a DocuSign-marked contract, but per Hudson Cook it "failed to offer evidence regarding who sent Ms. Fabian the agreement and how the agreement was sent", and its declaration never mentioned DocuSign, the verification process or the meaning of the data in the signature box. Arbitration was refused. Hudson Cook, https://www.hudsoncook.com/article/california-court-finds-business-could-not-verify-consumers-electronic-signature-despite-docusign-markers/ (read as search extract only).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Every completed document ships with a plain-language evidence summary a judge can follow without a vendor witness: who sent it, from which account, to which address and channel, what the signer had to do to open it, how the signature was applied, plus a glossary of every ID and field. Include a fill-in declaration template that the sender's own records person can sign and attach.

needs.need: Senders need proof that only the named signer could have applied the signature, because courts reject evidence that merely shows a login or link existed.
needs.who: Employers and businesses enforcing agreements (arbitration clauses, loans, guarantees) against a signer who denies or does not recall signing
needs.evidence: Ruiz v. Moss Bros. (Cal. Ct. App. 2014): issuing login credentials to all employees was not enough to show the signature was the act of Ruiz. Espejo v. SCPMG (2016) succeeded because the declaration detailed the unique username and password and how signature, date, time and IP were recorded. Garcia v. Stoneledge Furniture (2024): the HR declarant "failed to demonstrate that only Garcia could have executed the arbitration agreement". Proskauer, https://calemploymentlawupdate.proskauer.com/2024/08/employer-failed-to-provide-sufficient-proof-that-employee-actually-e-signed-arbitration-agreement/ and Ogletree, https://ogletree.com/insights-resources/blog-posts/california-court-rules-on-whether-to-compel-arbitration-where-employer-could-not-authenticate-employees-electronic-signature/ (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A single-use signing link bound to one recipient, never visible to the sender, plus an optional second factor (code to the signer's phone). The certificate states in words that the link was unique, when it was issued, that it could not be opened from the sender's account, and which verification step was passed.

needs.need: A person accused of signing cannot get the certificate or audit record from the vendor and depends on the other side to hand it over.
needs.who: People who say they never signed (consumers, ex-employees, spouses, property sellers) and their lawyers
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community moderators say Support cannot access an envelope's documents or Certificate of Completion and may confirm details "only if you are the sender of the envelope or were directly involved in the signing process"; confidentiality bars disclosure to third parties without legal process. One poster said the sender only briefly showed a screen labelled Certificate of Completion without letting them read it. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/in-person-signer-26695 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-111/how-to-prove-that-the-contents-of-the-document-are-exactly-what-i-signed-4317 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The named signer can self-serve the full certificate for any document bearing their email, after proving control of that address. A public verify page shows non-sensitive facts for any document ID. A documented route exists for alleged signers and lawyers, with a stated response time, that does not require the sender's cooperation.

needs.need: Senders need evidence that the email address really belonged to the signer, because salespeople and intermediaries create addresses and sign for people who have no email at all.
needs.who: Elderly and offline consumers; lenders and finance companies relying on contracts brought in by sales agents
needs.evidence: NPR (Aug 2024) on rooftop solar fraud: Emanuel Minto, 91, "didn't have a computer or an email address and says the salesman created an email and then forged his signature onto an electronic contract"; the solar firm's owner "confirms the salesman created the email address". Connecticut's Attorney General sued Sunrun and others alleging salespeople impersonated a homeowner to forge a lease. https://www.npr.org/2024/08/14/1244330369/solar-rooftop-panels-environment-fraud-deception and https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2024-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-sues-sunrun (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The record shows how the address was tied to the person: a confirm-your-address step before the document opens, a second channel the signer supplied independently (phone), and a visible flag when the signer's address was first seen minutes before signing or the signing happened on the sender's device or network. The sender can attach a note on how they obtained the address.

needs.need: When the signing happens on the sender's own computer or tablet, or with staff 'helping', the record cannot show that the named person rather than the helper signed.
needs.who: Employers onboarding staff at an office computer, door-to-door and showroom sellers, anyone using in-person signing; the signers themselves
needs.evidence: Bannister v. Marinidence Opco (Cal. Ct. App. 2021): the employee had not operated the computer during onboarding, no unique username and password was shown, and she "was not the only person who could have executed the arbitration agreement". Kerr v. Dillard (D. Kan. 2009): a store secretary helped the employee log in and allegedly signed for her. DocuSign Community: the certificate "does not provide proof of whether a signer was physically present at a device", and for in-person signing the certificate showed only 'In-person' instead of the signer's email. https://lcwlegal.com/news/employer-failed-to-prove-that-employee-signed-arbitration-agreement and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/in-person-signer-email-not-listed-on-certificate-2577 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The product detects and prints on the certificate when signer and sender shared a device, browser or IP. In-person mode names the host, requires the signer to confirm on their own phone, and sends the signer a copy to their own address. A signature made on the sender's device without that confirmation is clearly marked as weaker evidence.

needs.need: When the sender's account is closed, cancelled or purged, the signed documents and certificates are gone and cannot be recovered years later when a dispute starts.
needs.who: Small organisations and individuals who cancel a subscription or let a plan lapse; signers who relied on the sender's account
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community moderators: once closure starts you lose access; for a closed personal plan "those documents can not be retrieved" and DocuSign does not reopen closed accounts; users are told to downgrade to free rather than close. Clemson University IT: after accounts were deleted there is "no way to recover those documents". Another thread is titled 'My documents keep purging out of my account'. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/documents-for-closed-accounts-2516 , https://ccit.clemson.edu/?p=21782 , https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/my-documents-keep-purging-out-of-my-account-22945 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Evidence outlives the subscription. On completion every party receives a self-contained sealed PDF with the certificate inside. Cancelling triggers a one-click full export and a clear warning. Completed documents stay readable for a published number of years with no paid plan, and the verify page keeps working from the document hash even after the account is deleted.

needs.need: The vendor will not explain, interpret or vouch for its own audit record, so people in a dispute go looking for outside experts to read it.
needs.who: Litigants on both sides and their lawyers
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community threads titled 'Need Docusign Forgery Expert ASAP' (2025) and 'Docusign expert consultant needed for signature authentication dispute': a user already holding the certificate and subpoenaed metadata asked for someone to interpret it, help draft subpoenas and deposition questions, and testify. Moderators replied they cannot give legal advice; staff said they "don't have the ability to interpret or validate what a specific IP address means". https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/docusign-expert-consultant-needed-for-signature-authentication-dispute-27602 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/need-docusign-forgery-expert-asap-22760 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A public, citable reference that defines every field of the certificate and how it is generated, written so a lawyer can exhibit it. A standing business-records declaration from the vendor available on request at no or fixed low cost, and a published process and timeline for subpoenas and court orders.

needs.need: A sworn denial alone can send the case to trial, so senders need corroboration beyond the platform's own digital trail.
needs.who: Employers and businesses with many signers; their litigation counsel
needs.evidence: Barrows v. Brinker Restaurant Corp. (2d Cir. 2022, 36 F.4th 45): the employee's sworn declaration that she never signed was enough to create a triable issue, even though the employer's records pointed to an IP address the employer itself owned. Seyfarth's note: "electronic signatures by themselves may not be sufficient to enforce an agreement. Employers will likely need other forms of evidence outside of the electronic signature itself", and suggests two factor verification. https://www.seyfarth.com/dir_docs/publications/Law360-2nd-Circ-Arbitration-Ruling-Guides-On-Electronic-Signatures.pdf (search extract).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Cheap optional second-factor verification per signer, and a record of what happened after signing: completed copy delivered to the signer's address, opened, downloaded, any reply. The evidence summary lists these corroborating facts separately from the signature event.

needs.need: When two people share one email address (couples, a business inbox), nobody can tell which of them signed.
needs.who: Couples signing tax, loan and property papers; small businesses with a shared inbox; the counterparties relying on those signatures
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community thread 'I have a shared email address and the document was signed by my partner, how do I confirm that': replies say the certificate only holds the IP at the moment of signing, which is typically the shared home or office network, so it cannot separate two people; advice is that "sharing an email address between signers is not a best practice". In IO Moonwalkers (N.C. Ct. App. 2018) the audit trail could only show that someone with access to the business's email account opened and signed. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/i-have-a-shared-email-address-and-the-document-was-signed-by-my-partner-how-do-i-confirm-that-20176 and https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/using-e-signatures-in-court-the-value-of-an-audit-trail (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The sender is warned when two signers have the same address or a role address (info@, office@). Each person then gets their own second factor (their own phone) and a self-declared name and capacity, and the certificate says plainly that the address is shared.

needs.need: A signature applied by someone else using the signer's account or stored signature, or by office staff on the signer's behalf, can leave the relying party with an unenforceable document.
needs.who: Creditors, suppliers and banks relying on directors' guarantees; directors and executives whose assistants sign for them
needs.evidence: Williams Group Australia v Crocker [2016] NSWCA 265: an unknown person used the director's HelloFax account to apply his signature to a guarantee; he was not bound, and the creditor had not even known the signature came from that platform. Bendigo and Adelaide Bank v Pickard [2019] SASC 123: office staff affixed a director's and secretary's electronic signatures; the guarantees failed for lack of evidence of personal authentication. Law firm advice: keep a register of when an e-signature is applied and confirm who placed it. https://www.allens.com.au/insights-news/insights/2016/09/e-signature---a-case-study-but-not-a-test-case/ and https://cgw.com.au/publications/the-dangers-of-electronic-signatures-can-you-prove-who-signed/ (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A proper 'signing for someone else' flow: the delegate signs under their own verified identity, states the capacity and attaches the authority (power of attorney, board resolution). No stored signature can be applied by a second user. The principal is notified every time, gets a log of every use of their signature, and the recipient sees who actually applied it.

needs.need: Printed, scanned or flattened copies of a signed document cannot be checked, and the holder of a paper copy has no way to confirm it matches what was signed.
needs.who: Auditors, courts, counterparties and alleged signers who are shown only a scan or printout
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community: a user received scanned copies with an envelope ID but no timestamps or emails, and the sender said they only had a scan and could not provide the certificate; staff answered "there is no option to verify a scanned document" and another reply that "all of the security is only available in an electronic form". https://community.docusign.com/esignature-111/how-to-prove-forged-and-scanned-docusign-documents-20030 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/how-can-a-3rd-party-auditor-verify-docusign-signed-documents-printed-on-paper-731 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A short code or QR on every page leads to a verify page showing status, signer names, signing times, page count and the document fingerprint, and lets the holder upload a file to check for a match. The original sealed file stays retrievable by every party, not just the sender.

needs.need: People need to prove the document was not changed after signing and that a signature block was not copied onto a different document.
needs.who: Signers who suspect alteration; recipients handed a document that looks signed
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community: a user who signed on a third party's tablet and was given a copy on a USB stick believed one document had been altered and asked how to prove the contents are exactly what they signed; another reports a signature and envelope watermark copied from one signed document into another; others report a second envelope ID under the visible one and Adobe showing 'At least one signature is not valid'. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-111/how-to-prove-that-the-contents-of-the-document-are-exactly-what-i-signed-4317 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-111/someone-claim-to-have-a-document-signed-by-me-via-docusign-which-i-never-did-27308 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Each document is cryptographically sealed at completion; the certificate prints the fingerprint and page count of each document; the final sealed copy is automatically emailed to every signer so each holds their own reference; a free validator tells anyone in plain words whether a file is the untouched original.

needs.need: Timestamps on the document and on the audit record disagree or appear in a time zone nobody involved was in, which makes the record look unreliable.
needs.who: Senders and signers in different time zones; lawyers building a timeline
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community: the certificate uses the sender's account time zone, signer accounts default to Pacific time, a document finished at night was stamped with the next day's date for the second signer, and there are threads titled 'Incorrect date time of signing between actual signature block and timestamp in the audit trail' and one asking why timestamps in already generated PDFs changed when a time setting was changed. An Ontario case (Ahmad) involved an e-signature timestamp that differed from the time the signer wrote. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/the-date-stamp-for-signer-is-incorrect-21020 and https://community.docusign.com/general-discussion-145/incorrect-date-time-of-signing-between-actual-signature-block-and-timestamp-in-the-audit-trail-27370 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Every time is shown as UTC plus the signer's local time with the offset written out, identical in the document and the certificate, fixed at signing and never recomputed. The record distinguishes 'signature applied' from 'signing finished' and explains the difference in one line.

needs.need: The IP address on the certificate is treated as proof of who or where, when it often shows a mobile carrier, VPN, shared network or the sender's own office.
needs.who: Both sides of a dispute; judges reading the certificate
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community moderator: the IP may be an ISP datacentre, a VPN or proxy, or a mobile network, and IPs "provide a general indication of the connection source but do not pinpoint a user's physical location"; forum advice to alleged signers is to compare the certificate IP with their own. In Barrows v. Brinker the IP belonged to the employer. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/signed-in-location-23540 and https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca2/21-606/21-606-2022-05-31.html (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The certificate says in plain words what an IP does and does not show, labels the network type where known (mobile, corporate, VPN), states whether it matches the sender's network, and adds device and browser details so the IP is not the only clue.

needs.need: The evidence markers must be identical on every document in a signing packet, and the signer's name must appear exactly as the signer entered it.
needs.who: Employers and businesses sending multi-document packets
needs.evidence: Garcia v. Stoneledge Furniture (Cal. Ct. App. 2024, 102 Cal.App.5th 41): "Unlike the other documents, the arbitration agreement did not include an IP address or other indicators that it was executed electronically through the Taleo system", and the employer could not explain why the signature block read 'Maria Isabel Izzy Garcia' when that name appeared on no other onboarding document; she denied ever using 'Izzy'. https://calemploymentlawupdate.proskauer.com/2024/08/employer-failed-to-provide-sufficient-proof-that-employee-actually-e-signed-arbitration-agreement/ and https://www.aalrr.com/newsroom-alerts-4071 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Every document in a packet carries the same packet ID, signer ID, time and network details on its face. The name in each signature block is the one the signer typed or confirmed in their own session, and the certificate records where that name came from (signer typed it, or sender pre-filled it and signer confirmed).

needs.need: The record must show that the signer personally adopted the signature, because senders can appear to place a typed or generic signature for someone else.
needs.who: Alleged signers; senders accused of inserting a signature
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community: a poster says they were presented with a completed document showing a generic electronic signature they never made and never received the signing email (thread 'Multiple documents that have been fabricated and forged using Docusign with spoofed my email'); another asks whether a sender can simply insert someone's generic e-signature. In Aerotek v. Boyd (Tex. 2021) employees argued their printed names could not count as signatures. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/multiple-documents-that-have-been-fabricated-and-forged-using-docusign-with-spoofed-my-email-2362 and https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2021/06/enforcing-a-disputed-electronic-signature (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A sender can never place a signature in a recipient's field. The certificate records the adoption act (typed, drawn or uploaded, on which device, at what time) and an explicit 'I agree this is my signature' step, and says so in words.

needs.need: Senders need a record of delivery, opening and viewing, and of what the signer did afterwards, because courts often decide on whether the party knew of and accepted the deal rather than on the signature itself.
needs.who: Businesses whose counterparty later says an employee or agent signed without authority
needs.evidence: IO Moonwalkers v. Banc of America Merchant Services (N.C. Ct. App. 2018): the court relied on the DocuSign record of when the contracts were received and viewed and upheld the contract on ratification, despite a sworn affidavit that the owner never reviewed or signed. The ABA Litigation Section notes the contract was upheld only on ratification, warns the enforcing party may need additional evidence, and advises being ready to confirm e-signatures by affidavit and adding contract language supporting e-signing. https://www.americanbar.org/groups/litigation/committees/commercial-business/practice/2019/electronic-signatures-contracts-agreements/ (search extract).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The audit record logs sent, delivered, bounced, opened, each document viewed, signed, completed copy delivered and downloaded, each with time and device. The default document footer or cover text includes an agreement to sign electronically.

needs.need: The proof file must actually be produced and must be visibly tied to the specific contract, or the signature is treated as unproven.
needs.who: Lenders and businesses suing on e-signed contracts in France and other EU courts using simple or advanced signatures
needs.evidence: Cour d'appel de Besancon, 17 Apr 2025: the proof file allowing the reliability of the signing process to be checked "n'est pas verse aux debats" (accents removed). Cour d'appel d'Amiens, 15 Jan 2026 (Cofidis): a Protect&Sign file and a DocuSign envelope were produced yet the court found the lender failed to prove the borrower signed. Cour d'appel de Rennes, 21 Jul 2026: the first judge rejected the claim because the proof file was not linked to the contract; reversed on appeal because the file was corroborated by the contract and the debtor's ID. https://www.doctrine.fr/d/CA/Besancon/2025/CAP7B1D878EE889800BD9DD and https://www.doctrine.fr/d/CA/Rennes/2026/CAP2AE332BE6206762E49A0 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The proof file is generated automatically, embedded in or attached to the signed PDF, repeats the document's fingerprint and title, and the document itself carries a visible signature mark with the proof file's reference. It can be exported in the court's language and names the provider and the signature level.

needs.need: The signer says the request never reached them or they never knew the document existed, and there is no easy way for them to raise that at the time.
needs.who: People whose email was mistyped, spoofed or controlled by someone else
needs.evidence: Barrows v. Brinker (2d Cir. 2022): the sworn denial raised a triable issue about whether she ever received or became aware of the arbitration agreements, regardless of the signature. DocuSign Community: the author of the 'spoofed my email' thread says they never received the signing email; another could not prove a file was never emailed to them. https://www.shrm.org/in/topics-tools/employment-law-compliance/employer-not-compel-arbitration-based-electronically-signed-agreement and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/multiple-documents-that-have-been-fabricated-and-forged-using-docusign-with-spoofed-my-email-2362 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: Every request and completion email has a 'This was not me' link that freezes the document, marks it disputed on the verify page and alerts all parties. Delivery outcomes per message are stored. A completion notice also goes to the signer's second channel when one exists.

needs.need: Fraud and forgery reports to the vendor get no answer and no outcome, and courts may accept a disputed document unchecked.
needs.who: People reporting a forged or misused e-signature
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community: a user who reported suspected forgery through the vendor's reporting portal says the form states that no updates or findings will be reported to the reporter; another says they have not been able to solve the issue after contacting security; another reports that the judge accepted the forged document without verifying with DocuSign. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/verify-forged-document-3045 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/request-for-verification-of-authenticity-of-a-document-allegedly-signed-via-docusign-24778 (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A dispute process with an acknowledgement, a case number, a stated time limit and a written outcome the reporter can show a court: genuine and unaltered, not issued by us, or altered. The verify page shows a 'disputed' flag while a case is open.

needs.need: Users sign documents electronically that a court or statute will not accept in that form, such as court filings, deeds needing a witness, and company deeds.
needs.who: Solo lawyers, small organisations and individuals signing deeds, guarantees, declarations and court papers
needs.evidence: In re Mayfield (Bankr. E.D. Cal. 2016): a bankruptcy attorney was sanctioned because DocuSign signatures were not original signatures under the local rules; In re Patacsil (2023) followed it. UK Law Commission 2019 report: e-signatures are valid, but remote witnessing of deeds is not permitted under current law. Bendigo v Pickard (South Australia 2019) struck down an electronically executed deed. https://www.caeb.uscourts.gov/documents/Judges/Opinions/local/Mayfield-ForWebsite.pdf and https://cms.law/en/gbr/legal-updates/law-commission-report-on-the-electronic-execution-of-documents (search extracts).
needs.what_good_looks_like: When the sender picks or uploads a document that looks like a deed, guarantee, court form, will or sworn statement, the product warns by country that extra formalities may apply and offers the right flow where one exists (for example a witness who is physically present, signs under their own identity and is recorded in the certificate). No claim that every document can be e-signed.

needs.need: A basic email-link signature does not prove identity, and users learn this only when the signature is contested.
needs.who: Senders of high-value or high-risk documents (loans, guarantees, employment contracts), especially in the EU and UK
needs.evidence: A DocuSign Community staff reply: when contesting validity in court "a simple 'electronic signature' will not be considered valid, as this signature workflow doesn't prove the recipient's identity", pointing users to digital signatures from a trusted provider. A French appeal court (Amiens) noted that the reliability presumption belongs to qualified signatures, though non-qualified signatures still have evidential value. https://community.docusign.com/integrations-extensions-176/if-someone-forged-a-docusign-document-i-never-signed-how-to-prove-that-i-never-signed-it-5604 and https://www.doctrine.fr/d/CA/Amiens/2025/CAPA0E7645C754E21D6365F (search extracts; the staff reply is a forum statement, not legal authority).
needs.what_good_looks_like: The product states honestly, at send time and on the certificate, what level of signature this is and what it proves. For risky document types it offers an affordable step up (phone code, ID document check, or a qualified signature through a partner) rather than leaving the sender to discover the gap in court.

needs.need: There is often no stored proof that the signer agreed to deal electronically and could actually access electronic records.
needs.who: Businesses contracting with consumers in the US; consumers with no computer or email
needs.evidence: UETA applies only between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, judged from context and conduct (Vermont's enactment). ESIGN section 101(c) requires prior affirmative consumer consent with a statement of hardware and software requirements where a law requires written disclosure (FDIC manual). DLA Piper (June 2024) reports a federal court held ESIGN consumer disclosures and consent must come first for written TCPA consent. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/09/020 , https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-compliance-examination-manual/x-3-electronic-signatures-global-and-national-commerce-act-e , https://www.dlapiper.com/insights/publications/2024/06/esign-consumer-disclosures-must-be-provided-and-consent-obtained-to-meet-tcpa (search extracts).

The exact wording version, time and the fact that the signer opened the document on their own device are stored in the certificate. A decline-and-ask-for-paper button exists.

needs.need: Third parties cannot check whether a document they are shown was really completed, or was voided or declined.
needs.who: Banks, landlords, auditors and counterparties shown a document by someone else; signers whose voided document is being passed off as signed
needs.evidence: DocuSign Community thread titled 'Docusign is unwilling/unable to provide me with documentation that a voided document is being misrepresented by another Docusign user'; another asks how to verify authenticity of a signed document using the envelope ID; a poster argues outside parties struggle to verify and a court may have to order the vendor to validate a document and certificate. https://community.docusign.com/esignature-111/docusign-is-unwilling-unable-to-provide-me-with-documentation-that-a-voided-document-is-being-misrepresented-by-another-docusign-user-24960 and https://community.docusign.com/esignature-171/how-can-i-verify-authenticity-of-signed-document-using-envelope-id-23892 (search extracts; first thread seen by title only).
needs.what_good_looks_like: A public lookup by document ID returns the current status (completed, voided, declined, expired, disputed), completion time and fingerprint, with no account needed. Voided or declined documents are watermarked on every page.

needs.need: Senders are told by lawyers to keep their own evidence outside the platform, but the product gives them nothing to keep beyond the PDF.
needs.who: Small organisations without a records process
needs.evidence: The ABA Litigation Section advises being ready to confirm e-signatures by affidavit or otherwise. Seyfarth says a common error is failing to gather any evidence beyond the digital trail. Australian firms writing on Williams v Crocker advise keeping a register of when an e-signature is applied and confirming who placed it. https://www.americanbar.org/groups/litigation/committees/commercial-business/practice/2019/electronic-signatures-contracts-agreements/ and https://www.claytonutz.com/knowledge/2020/october/the-legal-ramifications-of-a-falsely-applied-electronic-signature (search extracts).

needs.need: Collecting location evidence exposes signers' whereabouts to the other party without their knowledge.
needs.who: Signers, especially individuals signing from home

mapped.need: Small organisations in the EU do not know whether a plain click-to-sign signature is enough or whether they need an advanced or qualified one, and vendors blur the difference.

README.md says the same under 'What is not in it'. The landing page makes no 'legally binding' claim. (src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx, consent stage, about line 672), and the adopt dialog says the mark 'is as valid as one made with pen on paper' (src/components/SignaturePad.tsx, about line 307). Under eIDAS Article 25(2) only a qualified signature has that effect.
mapped.suggested_build: Replace the consent sentence with: 'You are signing with a simple electronic signature. In most countries that is valid for agreements that need no special form. Some documents need a handwritten, witnessed, notarised or qualified signature instead. If you are not sure, ask {sender} or a lawyer before you sign.' Change the adopt line to: 'I agree that this mark stands for my signature on this document.' Add a /help answer 'Is this signature enough for my document?' with the three eIDAS levels in four sentences and the cases to watch (contracts that need written form, deeds, wills, land, anything a law says must be signed by hand or with a qualified signature). Link it from the pricing section of the landing page and from the editor's review step.

mapped.need: Users send documents that the law of their country does not allow to be signed electronically (wills, trusts, land transfers, some powers of attorney), and nothing warns them.
mapped.evidence_in_product: Nothing warns. The only check on what is sent is the filter for fake payment notices (readsLikeLure and fakeNotice in src/server/envelopes.ts). mapped.suggested_build: Before sending, match the subject, the document names and the stored document text against a short list (will, testament, codicil, trust deed, power of attorney, lasting power of attorney, deed of sale or transfer, title deed, conveyance, and the same words in Spanish, Portuguese, German and French). On a match show in the review step: 'This looks like a will / power of attorney / land transfer. In many countries, among them India, South Africa, Singapore, Nigeria and the UK, these cannot be validly signed electronically. Check before you send.' with a link to a new /help section 'What not to sign with Sign&Grow', which lists the examples per country with the law and the date it was checked, and says it is not legal advice. The sender can send anyway, and the audit trail gets the line 'Sender was warned that this may need a handwritten signature and sent it'. The same /help section is the home for the short country notes proposed under the Germany, India, stamp duty, South Africa and Kenya, Brazil, Australia and Mexico needs, so those are one page, not seven.

mapped.need: In Germany a contract clause that needs statutory written form is void if signed with a simple e-signature; the best-known case turns a fixed-term job into a permanent one.
mapped.evidence_in_product: No warning by kind of document or by country anywhere in the sending flow or on the public pages. The product ships no HR templates, and an account has no country. The only related words are general ones on /security ('If a law or the other party requires an advanced or a qualified signature, use a service that provides those'). mapped.suggested_build: On top of the warning for wills, add German and English HR words to the same list: befristet, Befristung, Kündigung, Aufhebungsvertrag, fixed-term, notice of termination, separation agreement. Text: 'In Germany a fixed-term clause needs written form: wet ink, or a qualified electronic signature, which Sign&Grow does not provide. A notice of termination and a separation agreement need wet ink. Signed here, the fixed term may be void and the job permanent.' Put the same paragraph in the /help list. Out of scope: offering a qualified signature, and any opinion on a single contract.

mapped.need: UK deeds need a witness who is physically present, and users need the signing flow to capture the witness properly; a remote or missing witness makes the deed invalid.
mapped.evidence_in_product: There is no witness step. The nearest things: the sender (not the signer) can add a second person as a signer and place them after the first in the signing order (routing_order, 'Signing order' in the editor), or use the role 'Signs in person', where the sender hands over their own device (role inperson). Text fields can collect a name and an address. Missing: a signer cannot add a witness from the signing page ('Assign to someone else' hands the whole signature over, reassignRecipient in src/server/envelopes.ts). There is no witness role, no attestation block and no words about being in the same room. A witness added as a signer uses up a paid signature (isChargeable in src/server/credits.ts). A separate one-time code for the witness depends on the codes being built now. Nothing flags wills or lasting powers of attorney.
mapped.suggested_build: A recipient role 'witness' tied to one signer: always routed straight after that signer, never charged, with a preset block (witness name, address, occupation, signature, date) under the signer's signature. The signer can type the witness's name and email on their review screen if the sender left it open. The witness's first screen says: 'You are witnessing {signer} sign a deed. You must be physically with them and see them sign. A witness on a video call does not count.' with a tick box that is written to the audit trail. Until built (S), a /help paragraph: 'Deeds: Sign&Grow has no witness step yet. A deed that needs a witness should be signed on paper or with a tool that records the witness. Wills and lasting powers of attorney are not suitable.'

mapped.need: In India a plain e-signature is weaker evidence than an Aadhaar eSign or a digital signature certificate, and users need to be offered the recognised method when the law asks for a signature.
mapped.evidence_in_product: Out of scope for a small web product: Aadhaar eSign can only be offered through a contract with a licensed eSign Service Provider under India's Controller of Certifying Authorities, with a fee per signature, rules on identity data and in practice an Indian entity. It is a regulated partner integration, not a feature we can write. What the product has is one method, a simple electronic signature by email link with an optional access code, and the certificate does record the method for each signer ('Identity check: Email link' or 'Email link and access code', drawCertificate in src/server/pdf.ts). Nothing on the pages says which Indian documents that is enough for. Sentence for the country notes on /help: 'India: Sign&Grow makes an ordinary electronic signature, not an Aadhaar eSign or a digital signature certificate. Where a law requires a signature, use one of those two. Where no law demands a signature ours can be used, and the party relying on it may have to prove who signed.'

mapped.need: An electronic contract is still subject to stamp duty in India and Indonesia; an unstamped agreement can be refused as evidence, and e-signature tools do not mention it.

What already works: an envelope can hold several documents and takes PDF, PNG or JPEG (README.md, 'Sending'), so a sender can already put an e-stamp certificate or a stamped first page in front of the agreement. Selling stamps through a partner is out of scope for a small product.
mapped.suggested_build: Country note on /help: 'India and Indonesia: signing here does not pay stamp duty. An unstamped agreement can be refused as evidence. Buy the e-stamp certificate (India) or e-meterai (Indonesia) first and add it as the first document of the envelope, or upload the first page already stamped.' Show the same two lines in the editor's review step when the sender's time zone (users.tz Asia/Kolkata or Asia/Jakarta) points there.

mapped.need: In South Africa and Kenya, where a statute requires a signature, only an advanced signature from an accredited provider counts, so an ordinary e-signature silently fails for those documents.

Where a statute itself requires a signature, only an advanced electronic signature from an accredited provider counts, or wet ink. Sales of land and long leases must not be signed here.' Add 'sale of land', 'deed of sale', 'offer to purchase' and 'long lease' to the warning list from the wills need.

mapped.need: EU and UK buyers must show where documents are stored and have a data processing agreement, and on small plans they cannot easily get EU hosting, a signed agreement, or a clear statement of what data goes to the US.
mapped.evidence_in_product: There, for control over what is kept: one free export of everything on every plan (GET /api/export), deleting an account removes its documents, audit trails, stored emails and files (DELETED_WITH_ACCOUNT and KEPT_AFTER_DELETION in src/lib/policy.ts, shown on /security and /help), and /security states that documents are not sent to any AI system. With no setting the block says 'Not stated yet' instead of staying silent. Have a lawyer write a short processing agreement with standard contractual clauses, and add 'Accept and download' in Settings that records who accepted which version and when. Say plainly: 'There is one region. You cannot choose another yet.'

mapped.need: Subscription card payments from outside the US fail: Indian cards are declined for recurring charges under Reserve Bank rules, and checkouts reject valid foreign cards with no reason given.
mapped.evidence_in_product: There: paying goes through the provider's hosted checkout, which runs card authentication itself. mapped.suggested_build: Let any account buy a one-off pack without the monthly plan: drop the plan check in POST /billing/topup for a pack of 9 or more, keep everything else that follows from having paid the same, and add tests beside tests/billing.test.ts. In the failed-payment email and on the Plan page show the provider's own decline message when there is one. Before launch, run one real subscription with an Indian test card in the provider's test mode and write down what happens. On /help: 'Card declined? Some banks, in India especially, block recurring charges from abroad. Buy a one-off pack instead.'

mapped.need: Name fields assume a Western first name and last name: names get split at the first space, family-name-first order is broken, and signers cannot fix how their name appears.

Tested: '山田 太郎' to '山田太郎' (a space removed), 'Иван Петров' to 'Ivan Petrov' and 'Sukarno' to 'Soekarno' were each answered with 'is a different name ... not another spelling of it'. (2) The first word is treated as the given name: the WhatsApp and text message share text starts 'Hi' plus the first word (shareText in src/components/sender/Recipients.tsx), the dashboard says Hello plus the first word, and a new workspace is named after the first word (src/server/routes-account.ts). (3) Default initials are the first letter of each word (src/components/SignaturePad.tsx), which gives a single character for 王小明. (4) Names in several scripts print as empty boxes in the PDF: see the fonts need.

When the scripts differ (Cyrillic to Latin, kanji to Latin) keep asking the sender, but say 'this may be the same name in another script, so we asked {sender} to confirm' instead of 'a different name'. Greet with the whole name in shareText and on the dashboard, and name the workspace after the whole name.

mapped.need: Text typed in non-Latin scripts (Chinese, Khmer, Arabic, Cyrillic) shows as empty boxes or unreadable characters in fields, typed signatures or the final PDF.

Tested with eleven signers on one A4 envelope (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/tests/out/map-nonus/A-page-1.png and A-page-3.png): the full-name field and a typed text field for 王小明, 山田 太郎, 김민준, สมชาย ใจดี, राहुल शर्मा and សុខ សុភា came out as rows of empty boxes on the signed page. The same boxes stand where the name belongs in the Recipients list of the certificate, and the audit lines read 'Signed · <email>' with the name blank; a name correction is recorded as two empty quotes. Иван Петров, Köln and Straße printed correctly. The signer saw their name correctly on the signing screen, so what was shown is not what was printed, and nobody is warned. Typed signatures are safe because the browser turns them into a picture (typed() in src/components/SignaturePad.tsx), but for a Chinese name the four 'handwriting styles' are four identical plain renderings (03-adopt-phone.png in the same folder). No test signs with non-Latin text.
mapped.suggested_build: Stopgap (S): in pdf.ts check each name and typed value against the font, and when a character is missing tell the sender on the envelope page and the signer in the review dialog: 'Our signed PDF cannot print these characters yet. They will show as empty boxes. Add the name in Latin letters as well.' Real fix (L): ship Noto Sans with Noto Sans SC, JP, KR, Thai, Devanagari and Khmer (Arabic and Hebrew too, for quality), split every string into runs by which font has the glyphs, embed each font subset only when it is used, and use this in drawField and in Sheet.text. Add a test beside tests/flow.test.ts that signs with Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Khmer, Hindi, Arabic, Hebrew and Cyrillic names and reads the text back out of the PDF. In the adopt dialog show one style, not four identical ones, when the name has no Latin letters.

mapped.need: Right-to-left text (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian) typed into fields is reversed, disappears or is left-aligned, and competitors treat direction as a manual per-field setting.

false_promises: Signing consent screen (src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx, about line 672), which every signer must agree to: 'An electronic signature has the same legal effect as a handwritten one.' The day is the UTC day, not the signer's: a signer whose own clock said 21 November got 20/11/2026 on the document, with no zone printed. false_promises: Certificate of completion (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/src/server/pdf.ts, drawCertificate): 'Identity check: Email link' is printed for every signer who has no access code. Tested: it is printed for an in-person signer who was never emailed, for signers whose audit trail on the same certificate says 'Not emailed', and for signers whose link the sender copied and used from the sender's own connection. For those people the statement is untrue, and it is the first line a court would read.

Certificate: the 'Sent' time under each recipient is the time their turn started, not the time an email left. It is printed for an in-person signer and for a signer the same certificate lists as 'Not emailed'. In a dispute about how the document reached the signer the certificate contradicts itself.

/security, 'No identity check yet': 'A signer is identified by access to their email inbox, plus an access code if the sender sets one.' Not so in three shipped cases: in-person signing on the sender's device, a link the sender copied or sent by WhatsApp or text message (Copy link on the envelope page, POST /envelopes/:id/recipient-view, embedded signing), and the access code, which the sender chooses and can read at any time. The honest sentence is: a signer is whoever holds the link, and the sender can hold it too.

Signing screen, consent step (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx): 'An electronic signature has the same legal effect as a handwritten one.' And the adopt dialog (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/src/components/SignaturePad.tsx): 'is as valid as one made with pen on paper.' These are blanket legal claims made to every signer. They are wrong for wills, deeds that need a witness, court filings and similar documents in several countries, and they contradict /security and the README, which tell people to ask a lawyer.

/verify 'No match' text: '<file> is not a completed document from this service, or it was changed after signing.' Tested: a genuine, untouched signed PDF gets exactly this once its sender has deleted the account, and at the same moment the signer's own link says 'We do not recognise this link. It may have been copied incompletely.' Both statements are false in that case. It follows that /security 'Anyone can verify a signed PDF' and /help 'Anyone can confirm it is unchanged at Verify a document' hold only for as long as the sender keeps the account, which neither sentence says.

/verify badge 'Authentic and unchanged': the check shows that the file is byte for byte the one stored when signing finished. 'Authentic' reads as 'these people really signed', which the check cannot show: in my test the sender signed for three of the four people and the page still said authentic. 'Unchanged since signing finished' is what is true.

/security 'Signed PDFs come with a certificate': 'who signed, when, from where'. 'Who' is the name the sender typed, attached to whoever used the link. 'From where' is an IP address, which is a connection and not a place, and can be the sender's own. Nothing on the certificate explains either.

Certificate, /security, the home page and the README on the audit trail: 'the history cannot be edited without breaking the chain', 'tampering is detectable', 'Editing any past event breaks the chain, and the app shows it.' The chain is a plain SHA-256 over each row with no secret key and no outside timestamp, kept in the same database (audit() and verifyChain() in /home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/src/server/envelopes.ts). Anyone who can write to that database can change an entry, recompute every later hash, and the app will say 'Record intact'. It catches a careless edit, not the operator. The only outside anchor is the chain head printed in copies people already hold. The other side's expert will point this out, so the pages should say it first.

/security 'Every step is recorded' and the consent screen 'each step you take': not every step. Downloads, visits after the first open, the delivery of the completed copy and the way the signature was made (typed, drawn, uploaded) are not in the audit trail. 'Viewed' is written once.

Home page, 'Proof you can check': 'Every envelope gets a certificate of completion.' Only completed envelopes do. A voided, declined or expired envelope has none, and the signer's copy of one says so itself ('It has no certificate of completion').

/security 'You get your copy, also later' ('Find my documents sends the link again to the same inbox') does not hold for someone who signed in person: emailMyLinks leaves the in-person role out, so they are sent nothing. Their done screen also says the document 'has been emailed to <sender>' and does not tell them that a copy went to their own address, although it did.

The 'date signed' on the face of the document, and the editor's line 'A date signed today is written as 2026-11-20': the date is the UTC date and nothing says so, to the sender or to the signer. Tested on a phone in Los Angeles at 5:30 PM on 20 November: the field shows 2026-11-21. The document then carries a date the signer was not in, and the screens (/verify, the envelope page) show times in the viewer's own zone with no zone named, so they do not match the certificate's UTC times.

Your fields stay where they are'). It also works on an envelope that is already out, and once someone has signed the sender is asked whether to have them sign again (correctEnvelope in src/server/envelopes.ts). The sender can add words to a page with a Note field and fill blanks with text, number or date fields that are prefilled and can be made read only (TYPES and PREFILL in src/components/editor/shared.ts); every signer sees them and they are printed on the final PDF. Not there: no way to strike through or cover printed words, and the PDF's own text cannot be changed. Word files cannot be uploaded (README, 'What is not in it').
mapped.suggested_build: A 'Strike out' field for the sender: a box dragged over a line, drawn as a line through it on the signing screen and in the final PDF (one more case where src/server/pdf.ts draws fields and in docField on the signing page), written to the audit trail as 'The sender struck out text on page N of {document}', and treated like a Note by the sign-again rule. Until then say it next to 'Replace file' in the editor and on /help: 'To change the printed words, change them in your PDF and use Replace file: your fields stay in place. Here you can add text and fill blanks, but not remove printed words.'

mapped.need: Month-to-month billing has to be available together with a BAA, with no annual prepayment or minimum contract value.
mapped.evidence_in_product: The billing half is there: one paid plan at US$9 a month, month to month, no annual prepayment, no minimum and no notice period, cancelled with one button or from a link in an email (PRICING in src/lib/impact.ts, 'The rules' in src/app/page.tsx, the cancel routes in src/server/routes-billing.ts, tests/billing.test.ts and its four siblings). The README notes that paying has only been tried against a stand-in for Stripe. The BAA half does not exist at any price (see the first need).
mapped.suggested_build: Nothing to build beyond the first need. When a BAA exists, attach it to the same US$9 plan and add to the pricing rules: 'The BAA is included on Grove, month to month, with no minimum and no annual term.' Until then the 'Not for patient information' sentence covers this need too.

mapped.need: Change orders need one authoritative current version, and lien waiver wording has to match the state and the contract.
mapped.evidence_in_product: There: an envelope that is out is corrected in place, so only one copy is ever in circulation. The sender replaces the file or changes fields, everyone whose part changed is emailed 'Updated:' with what changed, a signer who still has the old pages open cannot finish on them (the version check in completeRecipient and in POST /sign/:token/save), a replaced link says so and offers the current one, and the audit trail records each correction (correctEnvelope and describeCorrection in src/server/envelopes.ts; tests/integrity.test.ts). Voiding emails everyone the reason. Any envelope can be saved as a template, and templates are shared with the team. Not there: once a change order is completed, a revision is a plain clone with no tie to the earlier one (POST /envelopes/:id/clone; copyEnvelope keeps no 'replaces' value), so nothing tells the parties that revision B replaces revision A, and a new envelope does not void an earlier unsigned one. The Templates page is one flat list with no search and no folders (src/app/app/templates/page.tsx), although the server already returns template folders (GET /envelopes?kind=template); that will not hold up for a waiver form per state and client. The product supplies no forms and cannot know whether a waiver's wording fits a state or a contract: that is legal content and stays out of scope. An uncommitted change (src/lib/paperwork.ts) will remind a sender when a document mentions a notary or a witness, which some states require for lien waivers; it does not know state rules.
mapped.suggested_build: (1) Templates page: a search box plus the folder filter and 'Move' that the envelope list already has, so 'Texas, conditional waiver, progress payment' is one search away and there can be a folder per state or client. (2) 'Send a revision' on an envelope: it clones the envelope and stores replaces_id on the new one. On Send, an earlier one that is still open is voided with the reason 'Replaced by a newer version'; if the earlier one was completed, both audit trails and the new email say 'This replaces {subject}, completed on {date}.' The old envelope's page and its signers' links show 'Replaced by a newer version' with the date. (3) On /help: 'We do not supply lien waiver forms and cannot check that yours matches your state or your contract. Some states require a notary, which Sign&Grow does not provide.'

mapped.need: Charity discounts only reach formally registered charities, so informal low-budget groups get no help with price.
mapped.evidence_in_product: One public price for everyone and no eligibility check: free to start with 3 signatures, then US$9 a month for 9 signatures and US$1 for each extra one, the same features on both plans and one price for the whole team (PRICING and PLANS in src/lib/impact.ts; the pricing section and 'The rules' in src/app/page.tsx). Sign-up asks for a name, an email and a password and nothing about the kind of organisation (src/components/AuthForm.tsx). A community can also be given a code that makes the monthly plan free, typed in at sign-up or on the Plan page, with no paperwork (FREE_PLAN_CODES and findFreeCode in src/server/credits.ts). Worth knowing for a parent group or a club: the price is per person who signs, so one waiver signed by 60 families costs about US$60 (9 with the plan and 51 top-ups). The pricing section states that as a rule but gives no worked example.

false_promises: Landing page, 'Sign anywhere': 'Recipients sign from any phone or computer with no account' (FEATURES in src/app/page.tsx), and README 'No account needed. Works on phones.' Not true for older browsers, which the research names as the main source of signer trouble. Without Promise.withResolvers (Safari before 17.4, Chrome and Edge before 119, Firefox before 121) the document does not appear and the signing page shows the raw text 'Promise.withResolvers is not a function'. Seen by simulation on a phone-sized screen: /home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/tests/out/map-industry/old-browser-document.png. With JavaScript off the page stays on 'Opening your document' for ever.

/security, 'Only the right people can open a document. The people it was sent to, the person who sent it, and the admins of the sender's account' (src/app/security/page.tsx). Stronger than what is true: anyone who holds or is forwarded a signing link can open the document (the same page says further down that a signer is identified only by access to an inbox), and the people who run the server can read the files, which the app does not encrypt. No page says whether documents or contacts are sold or shared, which is exactly what agents, lawyers and clinicians in this research are afraid of.

Landing page, public forms: 'Good for waivers, sign-ups and consent forms', next to 'Every feature is on every plan. Nothing is locked behind a higher tier or a sales call' (src/app/page.tsx). No page says that there is no HIPAA business associate agreement, so a US healthcare practice can read this as fit for patient consent and intake forms. It is not: no BAA exists at any price, and /security itself says there is no certification and no encryption of stored files by the app. 'What this is not' lists other limits but not this one.

Landing page: 'Send one template to hundreds of people from a spreadsheet' and the comparison row 'API, webhooks, bulk send, public forms: Every plan, including free'. True as a list of features, misleading as a cost. Every person who signs needs one signature, the free plan has 3, a batch only goes out when all of its signatures are already in the balance (POST /bulk in src/server/routes-envelopes.ts), and an account that has not paid may newly email 50 people a day in its first week. A 40-person send means about US$40 paid before anyone signs. People who come from 'bulk send is locked to the top tier' will read 'including free' as free.

Consent screen at the last commit (7a716a0), shown to every signer: 'An electronic signature has the same legal effect as a handwritten one' (stage 'consent' in src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx). Too broad for the trades in this research: a lien waiver needs a notary in some states, and transfers of land and some healthcare forms need more than a simple signature. An uncommitted change in the working tree replaces the sentence with wording that no longer says this (consentWording in src/lib/policy.ts). Check that it is committed and that the README line about it ships with it.

Landing page, 'Reminders and deadlines: Automatic nudges...'. Automatic reminders are off for every new account and every envelope until the sender sets a number of days (default_reminder_days is 0 in src/server/db.ts, and the envelope page then says 'no automatic reminders'). A sender who relies on the sentence gets no nudge for a signer who filled everything in and never pressed Finish. In the same list, 'In-person signing: Host a signing on your own tablet or laptop when the signer is standing next to you' does not say that it needs an internet connection from start to finish, which a field crew will assume it does not.
